Devices and Software Considered
Based on the referral question and the student’s current skill profile, the following tools were selected for trial:

3. Kurzweil 3000 – literacy support software with text-to-speech, annotation, and study skills features.

All tools were configured to read grade-level sample passages from the district’s ELA curriculum and a Social Studies textbook chapter. Trial passages were comparable in length and Lexile level.

Trial Order: ReadAloud Pro first, then Kurzweil 3000, then Snap&Read Universal.

ReadAloud Pro:
J.M. required minimal instruction on how to use the device. He was able to scan a printed page from the Social Studies textbook and initiate playback within two minutes of receiving the device. He adjusted the reading speed from the default setting (180 wpm) to 160 wpm, stating that the faster rate was “too rushed.” When asked to identify the main idea of the passage after listening, J.M. provided a correct oral summary that included three supporting details. He also used the built-in dictionary function to look up the word “ratify” and was able to use the definition in a sentence. documents.title: AT Evaluation Report – ReadAloud Pro
documents.content:
Devices and Software Considered
Based on the referral question and the student’s current skill profile, the following tools were selected for trial:
1. ReadAloud Pro – dedicated text-to-speech reading device with OCR scanning capability, adjustable reading speed, and a built-in dictionary.
2. Snap&Read Universal – web-based extension for Chromebooks that provides text-to-speech, translation, and study tools.
3. Kurzweil 3000 – literacy support software with text-to-speech, annotation, and study skills features.

All tools were configured to read grade-level sample passages from the district’s ELA curriculum and a Social Studies textbook chapter. Trial passages were comparable in length and Lexile level.

Trial Results

Session 1 – September 29, 2025 (45 minutes)
Trial Order: ReadAloud Pro first, then Kurzweil 3000, then Snap&Read Universal.

ReadAloud Pro:
J.M. required minimal instruction on how to use the device. He was able to scan a printed page from the Social Studies textbook and initiate playback within two minutes of receiving the device. He adjusted the reading speed from the default setting (180 wpm) to 160 wpm, stating that the faster rate was “too rushed.” When asked to identify the main idea of the passage after listening, J.M. provided a correct oral summary that included three supporting details. He also used the built-in dictionary function to look up the word “ratify” and was able to use the definition in a sentence. J.M. reported that he liked the device because “it doesn’t look like a computer” and that he could use it “without anyone knowing I’m using it.”

Samuel Okafor recommended_AT_device ReadAloud Pro model. Record status: current.

Kurzweil 3000:
J.M. was familiar with the Chromebook interface but had not used Kurzweil before. He required step-by-step prompting to open the scanned file and activate the text-to-speech feature. Once the reading began, J.M. listened for approximately five minutes before asking to stop. He stated that the voice sounded “robotic” and that he had trouble following along because the text was not highlighted on the screen. When asked comprehension questions, J.M. was able to recall one detail but could not state the main idea. He appeared distracted and frequently looked around the room during the reading.

Snap&Read Universal:
J.M. was able to open the extension and select a passage from the digital version of the ELA textbook. He used the “Play” button to begin text-to-speech. He did not adjust any settings. After listening to a two-page passage, J.M. correctly answered two of four literal comprehension questions but was unable to make an inference. He reported that the highlighting was “helpful” but that the extension “glitched” twice, requiring him to reload the page. J.M. noted that he uses his Chromebook mostly for typing assignments and did not want to use the same device for reading because it was “distracting.”

Session 2 – October 6, 2025 (45 minutes)
Trial Order: Snap&Read Universal first, then ReadAloud Pro, then Kurzweil 3000.

Snap&Read Universal:
J.M. independently opened the extension and loaded a Social Studies chapter. He used the text-to-speech feature for ten minutes without prompting. He adjusted the reading speed to 140 wpm and enabled the “Read Aloud” highlighting option. When asked to summarize the section, J.M. provided a partial summary that included the main idea but omitted key supporting details. He stated that the extension was “okay” and that he liked that it was already on his school Chromebook.

ReadAloud Pro:
J.M. scanned a worksheet that contained a short reading passage and five comprehension questions. He listened to the passage once, then used the device’s “Scan to Read” function to access the questions one at a time. He answered four of five questions correctly. J.M. used the device’s bookmark feature to mark a section of text he wanted to re-read. He reported that the device was “easy to hold” and that he liked the “big buttons.” He also noted that the battery lasted through the entire session without needing a charge.

documents.title: AT Evaluation Report – ReadAloud Pro
documents.content:
AT Evaluation Report – ReadAloud Pro  
Client: J.M. (Grade 7)  
Referral Source: IEP Team, Lincoln Middle School  
Evaluation Period: September 15, 2025 – November 15, 2025  
Report Author: A. Chen, Assistive Technology Specialist  
Date of Report: November 18, 2025

---

### Session 3 – October 15, 2025 (40 minutes)

**Trial Order:** ReadAloud Pro first, then Kurzweil 3000.

**ReadAloud Pro:**  
J.M. used the device with a printed copy of a science article about the water cycle. He scanned the article and used the “Read Aloud” function to listen to the text. He independently used the dictionary feature to look up the word “evaporation” and was able to define it correctly after hearing the definition. J.M. then used the highlight tool to mark three key sentences he identified as important. When asked to explain the main idea, he provided an accurate summary that included two supporting details. He stated that he “liked the voice” and that the device was “easier to use than the extension.” He also noted that the device was heavier than his Chromebook but that he did not mind because he could place it on the desk. J.M. completed the session without needing assistance to navigate the device. He did not ask to change any settings.

**Kurzweil 3000:**  
J.M. opened a digital version of the same science article on the desktop computer. He used the text-to-speech feature and followed along with the highlighting. He did not use the dictionary or note-taking tools. After listening to the article, J.M. answered two of four comprehension questions correctly. He stated that the program was “fine” but that he preferred the portable device because he could use it in different classrooms. He also mentioned that the program had “too many buttons” and that he felt overwhelmed by the toolbar. J.M. did not request any adjustments to the program.

---

### Session 4 – October 22, 2025 (35 minutes)

**Trial Order:** ReadAloud Pro only.

**ReadAloud Pro:**  
J.M. brought a worksheet from his social studies class that contained a short biography and five questions. He scanned the worksheet and listened to the passage twice. He used the “Scan to Read” function to access the questions and answered all five correctly. J.M. used the bookmark feature to save the location of a sentence he wanted to revisit. He reported that the device was “easy to use” and that he preferred it over the extension because it did not require a Wi-Fi connection. He also stated that he liked the physical buttons because they were “big and easy to press.” J.M. did not experience any technical issues during the session. He asked if he could try the device with a chapter book, and I provided a printed excerpt from a novel he had selected from the school library. J.M. scanned the excerpt and listened to the first two pages. He reported that the device was “good” and that he would like to use it for longer reading assignments.

---

### Session 5 – October 30, 2025 (50 minutes)

**Trial Order:** ReadAloud Pro first, then Snap&Read Universal.

**ReadAloud Pro:**  
J.M. used the device with a printed copy of a short story from his ELA class. He scanned the story and used the “Read Aloud” function to listen to the entire text. He independently used the bookmark feature to mark a section he wanted to re-read. After listening, J.M. answered four of five comprehension questions correctly. He identified the main idea and provided two supporting details. He stated that the device was “helpful” and that he liked being able to control the reading speed. He also noted that the device was “not too heavy” and that he could carry it in his backpack. J.M. did not require any prompting to use the device and completed the session without technical issues.

**Snap&Read Universal:**  
J.M. opened the extension on his Chromebook and loaded a digital version of the same short story. He used the text-to-speech feature and adjusted the reading speed to 150 wpm. He did not use any other features. After listening to the story, J.M. answered three of five comprehension questions correctly. He stated that the extension was “okay” but that he preferred the portable device because it was “easier to focus with.” He also mentioned that the extension sometimes “lagged” when he switched between tabs. J.M. completed the session without further comments.
